tl;dr edition: neither good nor fun. do not buy unless its deeply discounted.

I can not refer this game in good faith. There are 2 major things wrong with How to Survive.

Firstly, take a look at the DLC. If How to Survive truly is an indie game, control of the project has been overtaken by greedhead corporate dumb think leadership. Someone (likely 505 Games) has opted to make DLCs out of basic features that should have been part of the basic game. Examples are an extra harder difficulty and a hardcore feature. Other DLCs (Heatwave) resemble what would have been unlockables for games only a generation ago. Lastly there are the DLCs that suggest the core game was released unfinished taking the cutting room floor scraps and selling them off as DLC when they got to them later. I don't know if the nickel and diming customers business model bothers you, but it sure as hell bothers me.

The second problem is the game itself. Its not good. How to Survive is a perfect example of the tidalwave of schlock being put out by the burgeonning indie industry. It is an inferior imitation of mainstream titles like Diablo and Torchlight. It tries to be unique and original with additional survival features like hunger, thirst, and sleepiness, but they're implemented in a way that make the game tedious and annoying. The quality is painfully amateur and inconsistent. Struggle as a melee character, but have 2 triple bladed boomerangs and you're so golden the game gets dull. The content is particularly slim. Each island is painfully small. And the game itself manages to be as repetitive as Diablo and Torchlight, but in the most flat, boring, and completely unrewarding manner possible.

How to Survive lives up to its lousy meta score. No idea why this game has such an overwhelmingly high positive customer review count. The $15 asking price with the lazy DLCs is crazy to me. Other games How to Survive is trying to be are the same exact price and offer more and better quality content minus the annoying survival gimmicks and DLC. Specifically either of the Torchlight games.

Honestly, my recommendation is to not buy How to Survive at all. If you absolutely must take the plunge, as stated in the tl;dr above, buy it when its 80-90% off. That way you won't feel too ripped off when you find out how painfully below average it is.

I picked this game up full price, from it's description it sounded like the type of zombie survival game I always wanted to play. Sadly it was a major disappointment, it's survival aspects in name only. All the elements are sort of there, the "open" map, ammo, limited inventory, food and water requirements and rpg stats, but their implementation is all wrong. 

 Few of them really matter, you get tons of ammo as drops, and managing water and food is pretty irrelevant, you quickly stack some items for that so that it's more of a petty maintenance than an aspect of survival.

The so-called open map is really just swathes of map with small pathways cut into them, with just a few open spaces that are usually there just for the sake of variety it seems. The only "Open" element is that of course it isn't a linear game and you can run back and forth between areas and quick travel between maps, but it's not far enough from just mundane backtracking.

The combat isn't too bad, it works for this type of game, if it wasn't for the overabundance of ammo and the overpowered weapons from the very start. Combat soon feels more like something you just do on the way and not much more enjoyable than running from place to place.

The crafting is another annoyance if you need a particular item, you have a limited inventory, that's okay, you shouldn't be able to carry everything with you.. but then there is no storage area. It's already not fun to run around this island aimlessly, I don't want to have to run around looking for that one damn ingredient, usually for a quest (what else is there to do in this game?) Just a limited item storage for SOME things, I can decide what to get rid of later, but a few times I've already dropped something I needed to find again, much to my annoyance.

The overall feel of playing this game was BOREDOM. I was falling asleep at my comp, I soon couldn't take it. It's not too relevant but the final straw was all the damn "Krovac's Rules" cutscenes. Think he's a neat quirky charcater? Wait till you have to endure overwrought, way too long, unskippable video tutorials with the same crappy music, for something that should be explained in 2-3 lines of text. 

Don't want to be mean, but it's kind of important to remember what a survival game is so we can actually get a good one. This just isn't it. It's very deceptive, because the gameplay it describes is far from the experience this game actually provides; a top down action game with bad map design and useless aspects that are little more than busy work, that drains the fun out of the concepts of crafting, exploring, or survival.

[h1] Once Bitten, Twice Shy [/h1]

A fun, 'Diablo'-esque Third-Person RPG, "How to Survive" caught me a little off guard. At $2.25 (Summer Sale 2014), I certainly wasnt expecting much but was pleasantly surprised at the quality of this title from 505 Games. 

[b][u]Campaign | Gameplay:[/u][/b] The story is straighforward - play as one of three protagonists stuck on a deserted island infested with zombies, and learn 'how to survive' long enough to find a way out. The gameplay is fun (and told from the perspective of a top-down isometric shooter), good graphics and atmospheric sound, M&K controls that are intuitve and responsive, features a broad selection of weapons (from Axe's, Machete's, Bow & Arrows, Molotov Cocktail's to a wide variety of guns), and interesting characters. The game's strength however was the Inventory setup - which allows you to collect a seemingly random mish-mash of junk from your travels around the island and combine them in various ways to create useful items (Eg. String and a wooden stick to create a fishing rod, An old bottle, kerosene and a scrap of fabric to create Molotov Cocktail's, An old rubber tire, an axe and string to create body armor etc etc).

[b][u]Flaws:[/u][/b] Uneven difficulty spikes, and sparse 'Save' points cause needless frustration in an otherwise enjoyable experience.  

'How to Survive' might not break any new boundaries but 505 Games have taken on a disparete variety of gameplay elements and executed extremely well to create a refreshingly fun, zombie-horror romp. At $2.25, this one is a no-brainer - A Definite Recommend (8/10)

How to Survive was the first game my first love invited me to play together. It was exciting—surviving on an island filled with zombies, scavenging for resources, and crafting weapons side by side. The game itself was fun, but what made it special was playing it with her.

Unfortunately, we only made it through a few chapters before she disappeared. Just like that, I was left to finish the first half of the game alone. It was a strange feeling—continuing something that was meant to be a shared experience, now just another solo playthrough.

Even now, when I think of How to Survive, I don’t just remember the gameplay—I remember the feeling of waiting, hoping she’d come back to finish what we started. But in the end, I survived… just not the way I expected.

TLDR: While this is no triple A game and that the DLC isn't worth playing, if you're someone who enjoyed Dead Frontier back in the day, you'll surely find yourself enjoying this title. 

Story: Not much going on here. Crash into the island, learn to survive, craft some stuff, do a few quests, try to escape. 

Gameplay: Like I've said earlier, it's much like Dead Frontier. Some may slap titles like Diablo or Alienation but How to Survive is way less complex than those games. This title almost borderlines resembles a browser game FFS. It's a top down, you move with WADS, aim by hovering your mouse over the head of your enemy, and 100% headshot as long as the reticle is red, a bit like Zombie revenge.... Wow those references are making me feel old. Melee is also horrible, though it can clear space in a bind, and is necessary on later islands. Crafting is a huge part of the game; weapons, healing items, food, quest items, etc, all require thorough examination of the whole islands, which in turn can become annoying or boring AF to one who simply wants to have meaningful content. Not to mention how harsh the inventory can be if you go through it alone. Each of the 4 characters have a different skill tree but I'm not really sure if it really matters considering there are obvious better weapons and they aren't the ones you expect. The campaign is playable co-op, and to me was the saving grace. I'm a sucker for unique experiences that make me drag someone else along through my horrendous experiments and experiences. 

Graphics: They're not as bad as how wonky the game is, I'm surprised to say it looks okay! 

Audio: Repetitive. Nothing atrocious though.

IMO, this is the kind of game you can have fun with a friend, couch co-op style. I had originally tried it on XBOX 360 with my son, but never managed to finish it with him. Time flies. Nearly 10 years later I thought I'd give it a finish. Still as dumb as I remember. KOVAC RULES. It takes around 8-10 hours to finish without doing any of the challenges and without going through any of the extra islands.

When I look at Steam Store Page of some product, and see publishers, how they put those positive reviews into the description, sometimes I just wonder what was that certain magazine or website thinking. Game wants to be either Dead Island or The Walking Dead, or even both, but as I see for majority of players it doesn't work and neither for me. I bought this game on sale, thought, what the hell.  What a pleasant surprise.  It's like Diablo 2 gameplay, with zombies/mutants as your enemies, and one of four survivors as your hero.  The gameplay is very fun, although it does get a bit stale with a lack of diversity among the zombies/mutants.  Couple the lack of diversity with a completely OP weapon (cough, triple boomerang) and you've got a recipe for boredom.  If you want the story mode to remain challenging, I highly recommend avoiding any boomerang, as they are fast, powerful, ammo-less, and there's no such thing as durability in this game.  Killing zombies with a shotgun made out of a tube and duct tape is much more rewarding anyway, right?

Still, easily worth $15 and a play through or two.  The challenges are were the challenge is (play on words intended).  You get your character dropped on an island with no equipment, a real "out of the freezer into the frying pan" kind of experience.  The challenge is reaching your escape under the allotted time, without dying obviously.  

The crafting system in this game is beautiful.  You can make guns out of tubes, boomerangs out of bones, armor out of tires, and potions/elixirs galore from the plentiful plants on the islands.  Very rewarding indeed.

The talent system is... meh.  It seems like an after thought, and there is a real void of any interesting talents.  Everything is just passive "make explosive arrows" "carry more explosives in a stack" "make X potions" "do more damage on headshot" kind of thing.  Would've loved some Dead Island-esque execution talents or some character specific special moves.

Bottom line: Buy it.  You can easily get 10-15 hours if the idea of a Diablo-ish zombie game with great crafting sounds fun to you.  How to Survive gets a 3/5.

I get the impression that I don't understand How to Survive.  The number of legitimate looking positive reviews indicates that whilst others have enjoyed the game I haven't.

The survival element from which the game takes it's name seems tacked on with little effect on game-play.  In the hours I've played I've never come close to starving or dehydrating.  A little message pops up telling you that you're becoming thirsty or hungry and that's solved by drinking or eating one of the many things in your inventory.

There are wells and bottles and canisters everywhere; I've haven't felt any tension or had to go on an epic quest to find water.  There are also edible plants everywhere so whilst meat might not always be on the menu starving is not going to happen.

Sleeping is ... strange.  There's no building or reinforcing shelters and no bedrolls or similar.  There is one special shack per island that has a closeable door.  That's the only place where you can sleep.  If you're 51% tired you can't sleep but if you're 49% tired than you must.  There's no wait command so sleeping through the night won't happen unless leave your character to get tired.

As survival games go there's no real element of survival in 'How to Survive'.  Fallout 3 with Primary Needs or State of Decay will give you a much better experience.

Would recommend if it's on sale. Overall, I'd give the base game a 6/10, and the DLC 4/10.

Pros:
Nice storyline. I'm not generally a fan of zombie games, but it's a mix of nature survival and zombie survival
Crafting lets you do different things without being too in-depth (though pretty linear/few overlapping components)
Plentiful ammo, so if you use it properly, no real need for time-consuming CQB once you get going in the game
Won't do any spoilers, but there are interesting twists and turns
The "Kovac's Tips" are a nice way of doing in-game tutorials; informative but fun and creative
The base game does a pretty good job of being clear about your goals, good map icons (though the DLC loses that in a lot of ways)
Overal enjoyable to play, and keeps you drawn in for the base game (though for DLC, see above point)

Cons:
The camera angles... it's a fixed cam, or rather a series of fixed cams that semi-randomly rotate. No way to adjust your veiw. Sometimes enemies will be a few feet away, but you can't see them because of the camera angles.
You need to stockpile all your "dropped" weapons in a couple centralized places, or you'll lose track of where stuff is - no system for keeping track of what you drop (no chests, storage system, or map to show where stuff is)
After the main game, not a lot is explained well enough - have to google A LOT later in the game
Lots of grinding later in the game, and though it says you're getting xp, it's essentially meaningless becaue of how the upgrades work
If you move offscreen, a horde of zombies could appear where you just were. Constantly clearing the map everywhere you go is a huge pain
Zombies respawn way too fast. If you can back-and forth between islands (or even off-and-on screen sometimes), everything fully regenerates right away
Nighttime combat: think Hyrule field from Ocarina of Time - no way to stop annoying pests popping up throughout the night, and from all around you. A bit of a pain to deal with throughout the entire game
Can't sleep through the night unless you're tired (at most, every-other day or every few). No way around nighttime combat

More or less detailed survival simulator + zombie grinder. Basically, survival part always puts you into some time limit, whether you have to find a place to sleep, or find food or water. But if you are careful and collect/use things around you in the right way, you'll deal with that part easily. Then comes zombie grinder part - you have to autoaim with melee or self-made firearms, trying either to QTE or headshot every zombie you meet. Sounds simple, but it can actually be a lot of fun. 

So, to pros:
 1. Maps are small, but very detalied, in very limited space of those islands, you have to run around a lot, and as you progress, seemingly same places become very different, as enemies and weapons change.
 2. Enemies are nicely done - every enemy is a threat if you ot careful. Even stupidest and slowest zombie can damage you if you miss and for some reason have nowhere to run. And armored runner is a lot more dangerous, not even talking about zombie deers and such.
 3. There are interesting recipes for different things - which you find throughtout the game. Altho, you can make those items way before you get recipes, which makes guides very useful. But in any event, you have lotf of options what to do with your things - for example you can cook and eat some meat, or make a trap for zombies with it.
 4. Overall gameplay is satisfying, killing tons of enemies is fun, inventory management is alright (not too tedious), crafting is neither too simple nor too complicated.
 5. Challenges and last difficulty add some interesting features to the main game - they worth checking on their own.

Cons:
 1. Biggest one - DLC's. So there are several things that doesn't come with the main game – those are Last difficulty, Nina character, 3 more islands and 2 modes – One Shot Escape and Barricade. And you need all except Nina, to get all achievements. A bit lame. But, on the other hand – If you buying this game with 90% discount, it’s not a big deal.
 2. One shot Escape DLC in particular – idea of it is, creating the most hardcore experience in the game, forcing you going for long time with weakest weapons. But there is a problem with randomness – because sometimes you can find all details for next weapon after learing 20% of the island, and sometimes it takes 100%. It’d be ok, if it always took 100%, at least that would be skill-based challenge, not luck-based.
 3. Barricade DLC is flawed too. Again, idea of it is ok – you trying to protect one point on a map. Except, it is always same point, same island, same enemies, and point you protect for no good reason right on the crossroads, not in some corner, where it’s easier to protect. Plus it takes literally hours to get even to wave 10. Maybe I was doing something wrong, but this mode is very strange.
 4. Well, there is a bug. If you somehow go into boss’ field of view, but if you are still far away (like behind trees, or on top of the mountain), if you do not get close to him fast (within 30 seconds or so), game can crash. Which can be painful in One Shot Escape mode, since you’ll have to start all over.
 5. If you play main game not on hardest difficulty – there is one OP weapon that kills everything. But only main game suffers from it, most challenges just don’t have enough items to create that weapon.

So, in the end, even with all those cons – most of them are about DLC’s. I guess it’d be more fair to rate every mode 1 by 1. + Crisp, minimalist UI
+ Excellent tutorial; fun, interactive, and does a good job of displaying some of the charm of the title
+ Voice-acting was of about average quality
+ Minimap is functional and easy to read; objectives and points of interest are clearly marked and hard to miss
+ Very detailed environment; the design and amount of inclusion is meticulous
+ Foraging is wonderfully implemented; by doing away with bold POI markers in the overworld, you find yourself constantly searching for familiar leaves, shapes, etc.
+ Except for a few small qualms I had with the crafting system (noted below), it is largely excellent; there are a refreshingly large variety of combinations
+ You have the option to 'uncombine' items that you've crafted, thus freeing up the materials for re-use; this little quality of life feature is incredibly useful, and I feel that many crafting systems throughout the gaming world would have benefitted from it
+ An appropriately moderate variety in creatures
+ Some crafting recipes are only available for certain characters, thus increasing incentive to replay
+ Exploration is both rewarding, and very much encouraged throughout the title
+ The story did a suberb job of managing to not take itself too seriously, without falling into the classic pitfall of being cringey and annoying
+ While the hunger and thirst meters fit well into the game, it was the fatigue meter that really stood out as a breath of fresh air; this added a bit more challenge and a greater feeling of urgency to the game
+ Hunting was very fun and challenging; tracking wild game through a monster-infested island could be quite the rewarding challenge

[h1][i]How to Survive[/i] is a short, -very casual- isometric horror-action game, unworthy of the survival title, and a major disappointment. Take its name to heart; in reality, the game is a glorified tutorial, with far too much hand-holding.[/h1]

The game regularly reminded me of the demo disks back when PlayStations were the rockin’ new thing, and I half expected the game to fade to black after a couple of quests and tell me it would be ‘Out this Summer’ in goofy Comic Sans. 


Initially, you select from one of three premade characters with predetermined stats, and character-specific talent trees.
There is another female character available by purchasing a DLC pack, but why this hasn’t simply been patched into the base game is beyond me.

[h1]-[/h1] The campaign plot is incredibly bland with your typical ‘washed up on a desert island and must escape’ theme. Expect a linear set of quests with little to no interesting objectives in between, a shallow sense of freedom, and an overall repetitive experience. 

All quests are fetch-to-receive with objectives and go-to points clearly located on the map, making the entire game far too simplistic to be considered survival at all. There is a visible % completion marker on the menu, and I couldn’t believe how quickly I was progressing through the main campaign whilst seemingly achieving nothing.

You can, of course, skip side quests, but there is so little else to do except mindlessly grind zombies on islands that are far too small, so I would recommend doing them if you do decide to play. I warn you now that they are borderline ridiculous, and if you’re looking for a more serious game you should avoid this completely. Monkeys and talking parrots destroyed whatever little immersion had been built for me and reduced it to zero.

Many dialogue boxes don’t match up with the voice acting. This is more irritating than game breaking but feels as if the voice actors were working on a different script. I could understand if it were worded differently for the purpose of a journal, but it isn’t, and as subtitles, it just looks unprofessional.

[A major annoyance for me is a continuity error with ‘Emily’s quest’ and a sound file. Maybe I’m being picky, but I noticed it, and it bothered me, so I’m mentioning it.]



[h1]-[/h1] ‘Kovacs Rules’ are scattered around the island providing you with tips as and when they occur in the campaign. The video cutscenes for these tutorials are unskippable and fairly irritating when you find a duplicate. This would have worked a lot better with a large tutorial island and a separate campaign map.
Zombie game Veterans will most likely be disappointed by this amount of hand holding. 

The difficulty also varies as you progress and feels uneven. I don’t consider this game-breaking but it is very disjointed with the overall tutorial feel. The combination of the two does not work well.

Certain survival mechanics such as fishing and hunting are largely useless, as edible plants and roots respawn frequently, and water stores are easily located on the map with icons. There is little to no danger of starvation or dehydration, making these trackable needs unnecessary. Rest areas and fire pits for cooking are also marked, dulling the experience further.


[h1]-[/h1] Inventory management is awful and very unintuitive. There are far too many steps required to simply move an item around in your backpack. Designated areas for food, weapons and craft mats would have been more sensible.

There are many craftable weapons which is a shame considering all end up feeling rather similar, not to mention certain weapons obliterate enemies with one or two hits. This allows you to cheese all the content and leaves all other weapons largely redundant. I’m looking at you, bladearang. 
You are able to dismantle certain craftables, however, so you don’t lose or waste materials if you craft the wrong thing or need the parts for a better item. This I [i]really[/i] liked. It’s been more than once that I’ve wasted rare mats and realised I already had three of what I just crafted, in several games. 



[h1]-[/h1] Graphics are probably the biggest positive; visually the game is very nicely presented, with a decent amount of detail, however, there are no in-game resolution or graphic sliders, and this must be done in a config menu before launch.

As for design, I actually really like the character model movement. There is a little bit of weight with each step you take - an overall sense of a backpack stuffed with items, aching limbs and exhaustion as you trek through swamps, scrub grass and jungle - it’s almost tactile.

On the flip side, enemy design is basic and mostly uninteresting, which is a shame. Just your standard bunch of corpses with different models and occasional movement speed tweaks, with a few behemoths thrown in here and there for good measure.

The day and night cycle is pretty cool, and things do get very tense with the nightfall soundtrack that always put me on edge. It does become rather grating at times, but it certainly lets you know things 'could get ugly' at any moment.



It feels as though development was hastily packed together, and never fully completed but still packaged as a ‘finished game.’ This becomes more apparent when you consider that various standard game content (difficulty and challenge modes) are available as DLC. I did not purchase these and so can’t comment on how well made they are, BUT, all -should- be part of the base game and not individually charged for, especially considering the store price.

More and more commonly now developers appear to choose the drip feed route, and slowly milk players with very small amounts of basic content rather than releasing a complete game, which I don’t agree with. Just do the right thing, patch the game, earn the respect of people you’re creating for (who have paid for your product!) and be a little more passionate [i]please[/i].


[h1]There are much better zombie survival games out there, and comparing this game to ones such as Diablo or Torchlight, is embarrassing. They are far better games in their own right, and I personally don’t understand why anyone would make this comparison.

If you have a limited amount of time to play games I would suggest avoiding this one. It tries very hard to be unique in its way of presenting a zombie survival, but seriously lacks campaign creativity and becomes very repetitive early on.

For the store price, [i]How to Survive[/i] is not worth purchasing. If you are able to buy on sale at an extreme discount (90% off) and playtime is not an issue, feel free to spend a few hours on it if you so desire, but I feel like I completely wasted my time on this one. [/h1]

You have ship wrecked and when you awake you find yourself surrounded by zombies and you quickly pick up a stick and the carnage begins.

How To Survive is a twin stick shooter of sorts with survival elements thrown into the mix.  The survival aspects in this are like you'd expect.  You will need to find and drink water, find shelter (and rid zombies of it) to sleep and kill the local wildlife to eat their meat so you don't starve to death.  You can even make fishing rods to fish as well.  

There is a crafting system and it was somewhat unique and fun in my opinion.  You gather up resources you find throughout the island(s) and you can craft things like axes, bows, body armor, guns and explosive devices.  You will also be finding plants scattered about and you can combine them and make healing items.

Herbalism ranges from making healing items, tonics for shields, better aiming and so forth.  For the most part all I ever used were the healing items.  Making shields and what not only lasted you 15-30 secs and it's gone.  There wasn't much threat throughout the game unless you neglected to upgrade your weapons.

Threats on these islands range from your normal zombies to zombies in full tactical gear to giant Resident Evil Nemesis creatures.  Even the wildlife can turn and cause more problems than the zombies do.  Zombie deer?  You betcha!  If you happen to die you end up leaving a tombstone on the ground.  There's nothing for you to retrieve, but once your friends log in they can see where you've perished.  I saw plenty of people I recognize dead all over the place.

There is a story throughout your adventure and your goal is to get off the island.  There are other people stranded which act as quest givers.  Quests are mostly just fetching items or off to see your next NPC that always comes with funny dialog.

The DLC consists of challenge modes, the barricade mode and an extra story line that takes place on El Diablo Islands.  The challenge modes are just that.  Complete certain game functions without dying and nothing in your inventory.  Barricade mode is you build a base and keep the zombies out of the base to protect a wounded friend.  You run around and pick up wood and make "barricades".

The base games story mode took me around 14 hours to beat and El Diablo Islands takes 3-4 more hours.  Max level is 15 and you can respec the skill tree 4 times.  The full game runs around $20 (including all DLC), but can often be picked up for $2 on sale.  Well worth it if the above seemed interesting to you.  Fans of this game asked the devs to make a 3rd person view and there is one availabe.  So, if you'd prefer to play this 3rd person over top down then check that one out instead.  It's the same game just different perspective.

It's a great time and it was great fun.  Always looked forward to finding my next blue print so I could upgrade my gear.  Recommended!

I've spent quite a bit of time surviving on the zombie-infested islands of How to Survive, and I have to say, this game is way more fun than I expected. At first glance, it might seem like just another top-down zombie survival game, but it manages to mix action, crafting, survival mechanics, and co-op in a way that's surprisingly engaging.

The story is simple: you're stranded on a series of tropical islands after a shipwreck, and your main goal is to survive while uncovering the mysteries of the archipelago. Honestly, the plot isn't groundbreaking - it's mostly a framework of justify exploration and combat - but it works well enough. The islands feel varied, from dense forests and rocky shores to small villages and hidden caves. Each area has different zombie types, environmental hazards, and supplies, which keeps exploration from feeling repetitive.

[h2] Why I keep coming back [/h2]

Despite its flaws, this game has a charm that keeps me coming back. The mix of crafting, combat, and exploration is addictive. I loved experimenting with combinations of traps and weapons, seeing which ones were overpowered, and finding ways to make zombie hordes more manageable (or just more chaotic).

Even though the story isn't memorable, the atmosphere and tension keep the islands exciting. You never quite know what zombie variant you'll encounter next, and the feeling of finally surviving a particularly difficult island with limited supplies is incredibly satisfying.

Playing with a friend amplifies the fun even more. We'd coordinate traps, share supplies, and try crazy stunts just for laughs. The game manages to make zombie survival both tense and silly at the same time, which is a rare combination.

[h2] Combat and Gameplay [/h2]

Combat in How to Survive is fast-paced and fun, particularly with ranged weapons. Crafting bows, guns, or throwing explosives feels satisfying, especially when you use the environment strategically. Traps and improvised explosives and another layer of creativity - sometimes it's more fun to set a trap and watch zombies destroy themselves than to fight them head-on.

Melee combat is serviceable but can feel clunky at times, especially when facing large groups of zombies. Still, the game encourages creative problem-solving: running straight at zombies is often a bad idea, so using traps, ranged weapons, and the environment is not only more effective, it's more fun.

Exploration is engaging as well. Each island has hidden resources, crafting materials, and side objectives. Sometimes I would just wander around to scavenge and see what crazy combos I could make, which added hours of replayability. The game rewards curiosity - you never know what supplies or interesting zombies you'll find around the next corner.

[h2] Conclusion [/h2]

How to Survive is a solid zombie survival adventure that balances action, crafting etc. It's not a hardcore survival simulator, but it scratches the survival itch without overwhelming you. The crafting system is incredibly rewarding, combat is fun, and local co-op turns the experience into a chaotic, hilarious, and surprisingly strategic adventure

If you enjoy zombie games, crafting and experimenting with creative ways to survive, this is definitely a title worth trying. The campaign may be short, and the story forgettable, but the sheer joy of crafting weapons, setting traps, and outsmarting zombie makes it memorable. Whether you're going solo or with a friend, there's a lot of fun to be had.

[b]You are shipwrecked on an isolated island, a desperate castaway in a total freakshow world.[/b]

[b]How will you survive?[/b]

Yes, how will you survive this mediocre "action-survival" game, a game which we've seen one too many times?

How to Survive plays like a isometric action-survival game (think of Diablo mixed with some minor elements from Don't Starve). 

Basically you run around, collect stuff you find while you mow down zombies with the collected stuff you've crafter. Usually with a rusty machete, chainsaw, an axe, a boomerang or some makeshift gun which looks more like a vacuum cleaner than a deadly weapon.

Let's just get it out of the way, the combat is extremely boring. It's boring, tedious and lackluster, and when you got thousands upon thousands of zombies chasing you then you'll get bored relatively fast. The developers also added a finish-move/take-down mechanic when the enemies health drops too low, but even that function is in most cased an hindrance for you to use.

The difficulty is also laughable. On the games website it says:  [b]"Try the “Iron Man” difficulty for a demanding hardcore game experience.[/b] 
Calling the Iron Man difficulty a hardcore experience is an insult to people who crave hard games. I died a few times because of my own stupidity (I used the take-down move and it got me surrounded), but other than that the Iron Man mode is a walk in the park. I never had any problem finding ammo, food, water or shelter.

There isn't a lot of "surviving" to do in this game, the crafting is tedious and the items you can craft are very limited. Craft yourself a triple bladed boomerang (with spikes) as soon as possible (on the second island) and you'll never want to use another weapon ever again.
Ammo, food, water and shelter can be found everywhere, it basically becomes a chore to survive, and that chore isn't even remotely fun.

The game also suffers from being ridden with bugs and is also terribly unoptimized. When you got an almost new computer with an i7 processor, 16gb ram and a 2gb memory card which has problems to render the water properly, then you know the developers were pretty lazy.

I wouldn't recommend this game, not by a long shot. It's simply not worth your time or your money.

Don't let the low metascore fool you.  This game might not be the best zombie/crafting/survival game ever made, but it has a lot to offer when playing co-op.  Even if the game feels as though it could have been bigger.  The idea of keeping your character fed, hydrated, and rested while exploring zombie infested islands and crafting useful items from scraps is a fun idea that is implemented well with this game -- the world, items, and crafting options just seem a little lack luster.

The survival aspects of the game, eating, drinking and resting, are presented simply.  Safe houses must be discovered and cleared out for the character to have a safe place to rest.  This part of the game works well.  The safe houses get progressively more difficult to clear, and they are spaced appropriately throughout the game.  It would have been nice if the islands were larger.  The player must search for wild edibles or hunt for food.  Foods can be cooked and combined, but a lot of the times there is little to no reason to do it.  While it's fun to make a dish a Fish 'n' Chips, there is no difference from that and just a cooked fish.  This part feels as though it could have used more work.  Maintaining good hydration is another survival aspect that is done simply and effectively.  Fresh water can be found around the island, and the player can store water in different containers.  These containers can be re-used for water again, or for storing other liquids.  Various fruits and items can be mixed with water to make "mix drinks."  This part of the survival felt as though it got more attention.  Every new drink that was discovered had different effects, and that led to more creative use of inventory space.

The back packs are a tad small; however, if you are planning on playing co-op, which I highly recommend, the back pack size works extremely well.  It took extra coordination between my partner and me, but that added a lot to the co-op.

The combat is solid and balanced.  What would be overwhelming at first, in time becomes just another brawl on the beach.  The learning curve fits well with the progression of the character.

The story is nothing exceptional, but that's not why I played this game.  However, all of the npcs are voice acted which is a breath of fresh air.

The asking price for this game feels right on.  It's a steal when it's on sale.

[h1]How to Survive[/h1]
[h3]Amusing and Straightforward Zombie Survival Game[/h3]
[h3]Worth trying![/h3]

How to Survive is a Top-down survival game set in a post-apocalyptic zombie scenario on a remote island. This game features an RPG system alongside basic survival and crafting mechanics. This entry also has an interesting visual style and a story filled with a subtle dark and absurd humor.

[b]Gameplay: Engaging and very creative zombie survival game 
Art: Great semi-realistic graphics mixed with a nice Grunge art style
Music:Unremarkable soundtrack with tracks that eventually become annoying[/b] 

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
How to Survive has a fairly linear story with several acceptable side missions inside a semi-open world of islands. This game features a day–night cycle system that has a significant impact on the exploration and survival mechanics. At night, exploration becomes much slower and more dangerous, as expected, due to the darkness and the appearance of a unique enemy that is honestly more annoying than frightening, but still succeeds in adding an extra layer of danger. Speaking of enemies, the game includes a somewhat limited variety of zombie threats. However, it includes zombie animal variants that pose a greater threat than their human counterparts.

The crafting system works quite well and it allows the creation of a wide range of improvised melee and ranged weapons, along with armor, explosives, tools, and food recipes. Each crafted item is unique and contributes to the game’s survival mechanics. 

[h3]Art and World Design[/h3]
The game’s setting is pretty good with a nice isometric format that allows a great environmental readability. This game features many different areas to explore within various islands. Each island features a unique layout of landscapes, beaches, villages and forests. 

[h3]Music and Sound effects[/h3]
The soundtrack is the game’s weakest point. Its musical ambience often goes unnoticed, and in some cases becomes annoying, particularly the nighttime music, which feels more like a harsh, repetitive sound than an atmospheric accompaniment. On the other hand, the ambient sound design is solid, the weapon sounds, zombies, footsteps, and natural elements are appealing and very indicative.

[h3]Additional Content and Multiplayer[/h3]
The additional content is reasonably affordable and quite fun to experience, as it adds new game modes. One of them, the Barricade DLC, is a tower defense–style mode where players must survive for as long as possible while protecting a defenseless objective.

The game’s multiplayer is fairly enjoyable and adds variety to the experience, although it does not introduce major changes to the core mechanics.

[h1] How To Survive - Review [/h1]

===

[h1] RATING: 6.5 / 10 - A generic survival open world game, with nothing awful but nothing impressive either. [/h1]

===

- Absolutely essential purchase
- Recommended purchase
- Purchase only if on sale
[h1] ->> Purchase only if on heavy sale [/h1]
- Avoid purchasing

===

[h1] The Good [/h1]

- Good amount of items to craft and discover, through recipes or by experimenting and combining stuff

- Decent amount of side quests

- Decent main quest plot and development

- Decent character skill system with no major unbalances or flaws

- Challenge mode and Iron Man mode to add other things to do apart from main story

===

[h1] The Bad [/h1]

- Short longevity. even with all the side quests, some of which are incredibly tedious, the game will not last you more than 8-10 hours

- Weak technical side, being a console port and having outdated and not really well done graphics and anonymous design choices

- No replay value, as choosing a different character wouldn't make all the quests and the progression any different, it just will differ by some difefrences in items ou can craft

- Unbalanced. Most of the time zombies will be easy to defeat with the equipment you have at hand, like machineguns, and plenty of ammo dropped by almost every enemy you kill. The skills just make your character more overpowered than it already is.

- Items do not have durability. Everything is indestructible, so you can stay with your strong weapons and armor all the time without having to make repairs.

- Body needs are very easy to satisfy, food is abundant as water, and their lack will not even really be crippling. You will never have problems on this side.

===

[h1] The Ugly [/h1]

- Huge backtracking will make you go around the whole map in the same areas over and over again many times.

- Quest rewards are mostly useless and can be found around the world easily

H2S is a twin-stick zombie crafting survival game in which you wake up on the shore of a lost island and must fight your way through the jungles to gather some survivors and escape. While it’s about as far from a unique game concept as one can get, How to Survive is finally a polished and competent entry into the genre. It’s far from a flawless game, but the voice acting is solid, the crafting has enough depth to last through the campaign, the game controls well with both mouse and controller and the visuals are very well done.
If you’re looking for a good survival game to satiate your hunger, How to Survive will be very filling.
